summary: Basic SIP security cannot reliably prove who originated a call or message, especially between different domains. This document defines a SIP header field that carries a signature over the caller's identity plus a reference to the credentials needed to check it. It replaces the earlier approach in RFC 4474.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like a signed note stapled to a letter that says who really sent it, so the receiver can check the signature instead of just trusting the return address.

subtitle: How a SIP network signs who is calling, so the receiver can check instead of trusting the From header.

tldr.problem: The From header of a SIP request is filled in by the user, so a recipient has no way to tell whether the claimed identity is genuine. That enables impersonation, robocalling, voicemail hacking and swatting.
tldr.mechanism: An authentication service authenticates the originator, builds a signed PASSporT token from the From, To and Date values, and adds it to a new Identity header field with an info parameter pointing to the signer's credential. A verification service recomputes and checks the signature.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8224 obsoletes RFC 4474, handles telephone numbers as well as SIP URIs, and leaves credentials and authorization policy to other documents. It was later updated by RFC 8946.

today: RFC 8224 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4474. It has been updated by RFC 8946.

sections.title: The Caller Identity Problem
sections.content:
In SIP, a user can put almost anything in the From header field. Without cryptography, the recipient cannot verify it. The RFC lists the abuses this allows: impersonation attacks that enable robocalling, voicemail hacking and swatting.

The existing SIP security options do not fill the gap. Few user agents have the end-user certificates S/MIME needs, and Digest authentication needs a secret shared in advance. Callers need to prove their identity to destinations they have never met.

An identity here is either a canonical address-of-record SIP URI such as sip:alice@atlanta.example.com or a telephone number. RFC 8224 replaces the earlier attempt, RFC 4474, which handled telephone numbers badly and signed material that intermediaries commonly altered.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can write any name on the return address of an envelope. This RFC adds a seal that only the real sender could have made.

sections.title: Authentication and Verification Services
sections.content:
The design has two logical roles. An authentication service adds Identity header fields to outgoing requests. A verification service (verifier) validates them. Either role can live in a user agent or in a proxy server; the RFC notes that a proxy is the typical home for the authentication service, because proxies are more likely to hold credentials and can authenticate registered users.

The authentication service authenticates the originator by prearranged means, then signs. The signature is carried in a PASSporT (Personal Assertion Token, defined in RFC 8225), a JSON object built from values in the SIP request.

Trust is the crux. A verifier decides what to do based on whether it trusts the credential the signer used. Authority over telephone numbers is harder to establish than authority over domain names, so the RFC assumes such credentials exist but does not specify a system; RFC 8226 describes a compatible one. Only SIP requests are covered, not responses.
sections.plainLanguage: One helper checks your ID and stamps your letter. The helper at the other end checks the stamp is real and from someone they trust.

sections.title: The Identity Header Field and PASSporT
sections.content:
The Identity header field carries the signed token plus parameters. The old Identity-Info header is deprecated and folded into the info parameter. The header may now appear more than once in a request. This RFC adds an optional ppt parameter (PASSporT type), alongside info and alg.

The PASSporT header uses typ set to passport, an alg that mirrors the header parameter (default ES256), and an x5u equal to the info URI. The payload has an orig object and a dest array, each holding a tn (telephone number) or uri, plus iat. If the SDP body has a=fingerprint attributes, an mky key carries them.

The iat value SHOULD come from the SIP Date header, and the authentication service MUST NOT sign if the Date falls outside local freshness policy; sixty seconds is RECOMMENDED.

The compact form carries only the signature, which keeps SIP messages small. The full form includes the JSON header and payload and is needed when extensions are used.
sections.plainLanguage: The note lists who is calling, who is being called and when. A seal on it proves nobody changed those details on the way.

sections.title: Signing and Verifying
sections.content:
An authentication service follows four steps. It checks it has authority for the identity (otherwise it MUST NOT add an Identity header). It authenticates the originator, for example with Digest. It makes sure a valid Date is present, adding one if missing. Then it builds the PASSporT and adds the Identity header with an info parameter.

A verifier works through its own five steps: skip an unsupported ppt, determine the originator identity, find the credential, check the freshness of Date, and validate the signature. When a request has several Identity headers, the RFC suggests treating the identity as invalid only if all of them are invalid.

Failures use SIP status codes: 428 Use Identity Header, 436 Bad Identity Info, 437 Unsupported Credential, 438 Invalid Identity Header, and 403 for a stale Date. After a 438 the authentication service SHOULD retry once with the full form of PASSporT, because some networks change Date in transit. A verifier MUST NOT trust the orig value in a full-form PASSporT as the caller; it always derives the identity from the SIP signaling.

What a verifier does with a valid or invalid result is local policy, outside this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The stamper checks who you are before stamping. The receiver checks the stamp is fresh and real, and says what went wrong if it is not.

sections.title: Credentials and Identity Types
sections.content:
The info parameter holds a URI where the signer's public key credential can be fetched. Every verifier MUST support dereferencing it, and it SHOULD be reachable by anyone on the public Internet. It also tells verifiers which credential signed when several parties could. The RFC mentions X.509 certificates and DNS-based approaches as possible credential systems, and lists what any credential system must specify. Signers SHOULD keep old key URIs available for longer than a SIP transaction, with a minute likely enough, after a key rollover.

Telephone numbers are handled by canonicalization: drop +, dashes and other non-numeric characters (keeping the hash and star keys), then convert to a globally routable E.164 form where possible. For SIP URIs, normalization strips everything after the host and port, removes any password, and lowercases the scheme, user and host, giving sip:user@host form. Domain authority is checked as in RFC 5922.
sections.plainLanguage: The stamp points to a library where anyone can look up the stamper's signature sample. Names and phone numbers are first written in one standard way so everyone compares the same thing.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Limits
sections.content:
The signature covers the From identity, the To identity, the Date and any DTLS-SRTP media fingerprint. Date and To stop cut-and-paste attacks, where a valid Identity header is lifted into a different request. This RFC removes the protection RFC 4474 gave to Contact, Call-ID, CSeq and the message body, judging them unnecessary for the main goal. The Via header cannot be usefully signed.

The mechanism aims at impersonation, not man-in-the-middle attacks. An attacker can simply strip the Identity header, so a missing header cannot be the sole basis for a decision. The value of an assurance is limited by how well the signing domain authenticates its users, and the display name in From is not covered. Direct TLS to the authentication service SHOULD be used where possible.

On privacy, the mechanism adds no information to requests beyond showing that a service will sign for the originator. Anonymous URIs such as sip:anonymous@example.com can be signed, but the domain must be one the signer holds a credential for. The full form of PASSporT could reveal a canonicalized number not otherwise visible.
sections.plainLanguage: The seal stops people reusing a note meant for someone else. It cannot stop a thief ripping the note off, and it is only as good as the stamper who made it.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 4474
sections.content:
The RFC says the original Identity header is not believed to have been deployed or even implemented in deployed products, so it contains no backwards-compatibility provisions. The salient changes are:

  • The credential mechanism is generalized; enrollment, acquisition and trust are out of scope.
  • The signature no longer covers CSeq, Call-ID, Contact or the message body, but does cover key fingerprints in SDP.
  • Identity-Info is deprecated and becomes parameters of Identity, which can now appear several times.
  • The signed digest format is replaced by PASSporT.
  • Status code descriptions are revised.

IANA changed the reason phrases of 436 and 437 and deprecated the old algorithm registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The first try did not fit how phone systems really work, so this version rebuilds it with a standard token and a simpler plan.

SIP RESPONSE CODES USED BY VERIFIERS

items.label: Use Identity Header
items.desc: An Identity header is required by policy but none usable was received.

items.label: Bad Identity Info
items.desc: The credential named in info could not be acquired.

items.label: Unsupported Credential
items.desc: The credential was found but is not supported, for example an untrusted CA.

items.label: Invalid Identity Header
items.desc: No Identity header with a valid, supported PASSporT was received.

items.label: Stale Date
items.desc: The Date or iat value is older than local freshness policy allows.
